summary: DAGent (NYU / NYU Shanghai; accepted at NeurIPS 2026 per the arXiv comment) is a deep-research multi-agent framework in which an Orchestrator grows a task DAG one batch at a time ('Evaluate-then-Grow'), conditioning each expansion on confidence and uncertainty signals from completed nodes, instead of committing a full plan upfront and patching it ('Plan-then-Patch'). ReAct Executors run each node in its own context; compact QueryDocs are propagated selectively along edges, with full transcripts recallable on demand. DAGRPO adds topology-aware credit and a structural-compliance regulariser to GRPO. On BrowseComp-Plus (150), GAIA text-only (103) and xbench-DeepSearch (100), with the same backbone and tool stack for all methods, DAGent on Qwen3-32B scores 47.3/55.3/65.0 vs 43.3/51.5/63.0 for FlowSearch (another DAG system) and 31.3/39.8/58.0 for ReAct at 109K context. A same-architecture ablation shows a single upfront plan (43.7 overall) is no better than plain ReAct (~43.0), while incremental growth reaches 55.9. DAGRPO adds 3.0 points over GRPO on Qwen3-8B (three seeds). Code and prompts are released; the LLM judge is human-validated (kappa=0.95).

claims.claim: DAGent consistently outperforms the strongest training-free baselines across backbones from Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-235B-A22B
claims.evidence: Table 1, single greedy pass per cell: at Qwen3-32B +4.0/+3.8/+2.0 over FlowSearch and +6.0/+10.6/+7.0 over the best non-DAG baseline; at 235B +5.3/+5.8/+2.0 over the best open-source baseline, but FlowSearch was not run there. Figure 3 / Table 9 replicate the top position on Seed-OSS-36B, GLM-4-32B and Nemotron-3-Nano-30B. No CIs; on 100-150 items a 2-4 point gap is 2-6 questions.

claims.claim: Evidence-conditioned incremental planning beats Plan-then-Patch, which beats a single upfront plan
claims.evidence: Table 2 (Qwen3-32B, same architecture): Plan-then-Patch costs 5.3/4.8/4.0 points; a single upfront plan with no replanning costs a further 8.7/7.8/6.0 (overall 55.9 -> 51.2 -> 43.7). Single pass; the Plan-then-Patch variant is the authors' own construction.

claims.claim: The gains come from more targeted evidence expansion rather than additional computation
claims.evidence: True relative to the Plan-then-Patch variant (1.20M vs 1.68M tokens, 541.6 vs 731.9 s on BrowseComp-Plus) and FlowSearch (1.57M). DAGent uses 32% more tokens than Flash-Searcher (0.91M). Token totals for the linear ReAct, Summary and Fold baselines are not reported, so 'not more computation' is unverified against non-DAG agents.

claims.claim: The lead extends to GPT-5 at 327K context
claims.evidence: Figure 4 compares DAGent on GPT-5 with baseline numbers reproduced from other papers (Sun et al., Qin et al., Hu et al.), including systems on different models (e.g. FlowSearch on o4-mini) and tool stacks; GAIA here is the full 165-task set with a multimodal extension.

claims.claim: DAGRPO improves over a same-budget outcome-only GRPO baseline by 3.0 average Pass@1
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B, LoRA, 21 update steps, three seeds with SDs: 49.6/53.4/65.7 vs 46.0/50.8/63.0. Component ablations (Table 3) use a single training seed. App. F concedes scale and schedule generality are untested.
claims.location: §4.2, Table 1, Table 3, App. E, App. F

claims.claim: Selective Propagation and QueryDocs are necessary context components
claims.evidence: Removing Selective Propagation costs 12.6/10.6/8.0 points, QueryDoc 8.0/7.7/5.0, InteractionTranscript (and RecallTool) 4.0/2.9/2.0 (Table 2, single pass).

patterns.note: Scoped to deep-research QA. Comparison: same backbone and tool stack vs plain ReAct (32K/109K), Summary and Fold agents and two DAG systems; DAGent wins on all three benchmarks and five backbones. The within-architecture ablation shows the generation policy is what matters: an LLM DAG committed upfront (43.7) is no better than ReAct (~43.0), and only evidence-conditioned incremental growth wins (55.9). Caveats: single greedy pass, and the linear baselines' total tokens are not reported, so budget parity with plain loops is unverified (it is shown against the plan-then-patch variant and FlowSearch).
Orchestrator-plus-executors works only when planning is interleaved with evidence; the upfront planner-executor variant equals a plain loop (Table 2).
ReAct-109K trails DAGent by 6-16 points at Qwen3-32B, but matches DAGent's own single-upfront-plan variant; a plain loop is a fair default against committed DAGs.
Same-architecture ablation: replacing compact QueryDocs costs 5.0-8.0 points and dropping selective propagation 8.0-12.6 (Table 2).
Narrow: DAGRPO beats GRPO by 3.0 average points with the same budget on Qwen3-8B, LoRA, 21 steps, three seeds.
No static workflow is evaluated; the paper argues fixed plans are brittle when findings redirect the search, and its upfront-plan ablation is the closest proxy.
Per-task tokens, tool calls and time reported for DAG variants (Table 10); no budget control mechanism and no linear-baseline costs.
GPT-4o-mini judge validated against three humans on 150 tuples (kappa=0.95, App. C.5); closed-form answers make judging easy.

methodology.sample: BrowseComp-Plus 150 (fixed corpus), GAIA 103 text-only (Level 3 only 12), xbench-DeepSearch 100; GAIA full 165 for the GPT-5 figure
methodology.baselines: ReAct 32K/109K, Summary agent, Fold agent, Flash-Searcher, FlowSearch, all with the same backbone and tool stack; Plan-then-Patch and single-plan ablations; GRPO for RL
methodology.models: Qwen3-8B/32B/235B-A22B; Seed-OSS-36B, GLM-4-32B, Nemotron-3-Nano-30B spot check; GPT-5 at 327K; GPT-4o-mini judge
methodology.variance: Training-free results and prompt-layer ablations are a single greedy pass; RL main rows three seeds with SD; RL component ablations one seed
methodology.ablations: Planning policy (incremental / patch / upfront), context components, DAGRPO components and alpha
methodology.contamination_controls: BrowseComp-Plus uses a fixed verified corpus; GAIA and xbench use live Google search via Serper with no answer-leak filtering described
methodology.languages: English and Chinese web QA; no code

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/hanwenliu6825/DAGent; all prompts verbatim in App. G; parameters in App. C

biases.detail: Training-free comparisons and Table 2 ablations are one greedy pass; 2-5 point gaps on 100-150 items lack CIs.
GAIA and xbench answers are discoverable via live web search; no leak filtering described.
Token and time totals are given only for DAG workflows; linear baselines' costs are omitted, so compute parity with plain loops is not shown.
Plan-then-Patch, the main foil, is the authors' own variant of their system.
GAIA text-only has 103 items, 12 at Level 3.
The GPT-5 frontier comparison uses baseline numbers from other papers with different models and tool stacks.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Open-weight Qwen, Seed-OSS, GLM and Nemotron models; GPT-5 and GPT-4o-mini via API
coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating their own open-source method; no commercial product.

verdict_reason: Same-backbone, same-tool comparisons against strong linear and DAG baselines, a clean within-architecture ablation of the planning policy, a human-validated judge, multi-backbone replication, released code and prompts, and a stated limitations section. Remaining weaknesses (single-pass training-free numbers, unreported linear-baseline cost, cross-paper GPT-5 numbers) narrow the claims but do not undercut the central finding that evidence-conditioned DAG growth beats upfront DAGs and plain loops on deep-research QA.
applicability: The most direct evidence in this batch on the team's DAG question, though the domain is web research, not Java code. It implies that if the team uses LLM-generated task DAGs, they should be grown incrementally from verified intermediate results, such as discovering which of the several repositories a schema change touches before planning the per-repo edits. Committing a full DAG from the spec upfront performed no better than a plain agent loop and wasted 40% more tokens than incremental growth. Passing compact per-node summaries (QueryDoc-style) rather than full transcripts between nodes is also supported. It does not show that DAGs beat a single loop on code-editing tasks, where tests and compilers already provide the evidence a loop reacts to.

conflicts_with.detail: ATG reports an LLM-compiled upfront DAG beating ReAct by 30-55 points (same model and action budget), whereas DAGent's single-upfront-plan variant only matches ReAct. ATG's extra LLM calls are uncounted and its ReAct baseline looks weak.
G-ReAct credits a fixed-topology query graph with deep-search gains; DAGent's ablation finds pre-committed structure helps little unless the graph grows from evidence.
Agree in direction: E3-Orch also trains a DAG orchestrator with structure-aware RL and reports gains over orchestration baselines, consistent with DAGRPO's +3.0 over GRPO.

Same batch: CAIRN also grows its DAG incrementally but costs 3.7-14.7x a single loop's tokens; DAGent reports lower tokens than its plan-then-patch variant but omits linear-baseline costs, so the two papers leave DAG-vs-loop cost unresolved.
